idiom_name: struct with a protected name/value partition + AES-256-GCM sealing over OpenSSL EVP or libsodium secretbox
implementation_notes: C has no classes, no serialization and no cryptographic library in the language itself, so the Obfuscated Transfer Object is hand-written: a struct keeps the unprotected pairs inline and the protected pairs in a separate map/array that is serialized and sealed with an AEAD - OpenSSL's EVP_EncryptInit_ex/EVP_EncryptUpdate/EVP_EncryptFinal_ex with AES-256-GCM, or libsodium's crypto_secretbox_easy - while a dedicated printer renders only the unprotected partition. What replaces the classic structure: the seal/open function pair plus the redaction table replace the class's protected map and masked list, and every serializer, logger and debugger has to be taught the contract by hand because nothing in the language enforces it. Use the masked-list route (print filter only, no crypto) when the threat is accidental logging; use the AEAD route when the object travels through code you do not trust.
pitfalls: Nothing stops a caller from reading the plaintext partition while it exists: seal as soon as the values are set, keep the plaintext in a local, and wipe it (OPENSSL_cleanse / sodium_memzero) before it goes out of scope.
A log path that walks the struct field by field silently bypasses oto_print; the redaction contract lives only in documentation and every serializer must be reviewed by hand.
AEAD nonces must never repeat under one key: store the nonce with the ciphertext and generate it with RAND_bytes/randombytes_buf - a fixed nonce destroys GCM's confidentiality and authentication.
Key bytes read from a file or the environment stay in process memory and cannot be reliably wiped afterwards; prefer a key handle/HSM when the deployment offers one and keep key buffers short-lived.
